name: Mechanical engineer
summary: Mechanical engineering interviews usually test whether you understand the fundamentals well enough to use them: strength of materials, thermodynamics, manufacturing processes, machine design and drawings, applied to practical problems. Candidates commonly report questions on their final-year project or internship, a written or online technical test at many companies and, for experienced roles, deeper questions on the machines, processes or designs they've owned.
rounds: Online or written test: aptitude and mechanical subjects (at many companies and campus drives)
Technical interview on core subjects, your project and internships
Practical or drawing questions for some roles, such as reading a drawing or a short CAD task
For experienced roles, a discussion with the plant, design or maintenance manager on past work
HR round, often covering relocation and shift or site work
looks_for: Fundamentals you can explain in plain words and apply
Practical sense: how parts are made, how they fail and how they're maintained
Reading drawings, tolerances and fits, especially for design roles
Safety awareness on the shop floor
Owning your project and internship work

questions.text: Tell me about your final-year project or internship. What was your part, and what problem did you solve?
covers: The problem and why it mattered
Your own work: calculations, design, fabrication or testing
The result, its limits and what you'd change

questions.text: Tell me about a time something you designed or built didn't work the first time.
covers: What went wrong and how you found out
How you worked out the cause
The fix and what you'd check earlier next time

questions.text: Describe a time you worked with technicians or operators to solve a problem.
covers: The problem and what they knew that you didn't
How you listened and shared the work
The fix and what you learned from them

questions.text: Tell me about a time you had to learn a new tool or software quickly, such as a CAD package.
covers: Why you needed it and how little time you had
How you learned it
What you produced with it

questions.text: A shaft in a machine keeps breaking after a few months of use. How would you work out why?
covers: Looking at the break: where it happened, such as a keyway or a step, and what the surface shows
Checking loads, alignment, material and whether repeated stress is causing fatigue
Fixes such as a larger fillet radius, a better material or alignment, and how you'd confirm them

questions.text: What does a stress-strain curve tell you about a material, and how does that help when choosing one?
covers: The elastic region, yield point, ultimate strength and fracture
The difference between ductile and brittle behaviour
Choosing a material and safety margin for the expected load

questions.text: Why does an engine or electric motor need cooling, and how does heat leave it?
covers: Heat from combustion or losses raises temperatures that damage parts and lubricants
Conduction through metal, convection to coolant or air, and radiation from hot surfaces
Signs that cooling is failing and what you'd check

questions.text: Compare casting, forging and machining. When would you choose each for a part?
covers: Casting for complex or large shapes; forging for strength under heavy load
Machining for accurate features and finishes, often after casting or forging
How volume, cost and required strength drive the choice, with an example part

questions.text: Why do drawings carry tolerances and fits? Give me an example of a clearance fit and an interference fit.
covers: No part is made exactly to size; tolerances say what's acceptable
Clearance: a shaft that must turn freely in a bush; interference: a bearing or gear pressed onto a shaft
Tighter tolerances cost more, so use them only where the function needs them

questions.text: A pump's output has dropped and it has become noisy. What would you check?
covers: The suction side: blockages, low liquid level, air getting in, signs of cavitation
Wear and alignment: impeller, seals, bearings and coupling to the motor
Isolating it safely before inspection, and testing performance after the fix

questions.text: What's the difference between breakdown, preventive and predictive maintenance?
covers: Breakdown: fix after failure; preventive: service on a schedule
Predictive: act on condition data such as vibration, temperature or oil analysis
Choosing by how critical the machine is and what a failure would cost

questions.text: Explain how a refrigerator or air conditioner moves heat, in simple words.
covers: The refrigerant absorbs heat as it evaporates in the evaporator inside
The compressor raises its pressure and temperature; the condenser gives that heat off outside
The expansion valve drops the pressure so the cycle can repeat

questions.text: A production line is rejecting too many parts. How would you bring the rejection rate down?
covers: Data first: which defect, and on which machine, shift or batch
Root-cause tools such as a fishbone diagram or the 5 Whys
Fixing the cause and checking with data that the fix holds

questions.text: How would you choose a material for a bracket that must be light but strong?
covers: The loads, environment, temperature and how many parts are needed
Options such as aluminium alloys, steel or plastics, compared on strength for their weight and cost
How the manufacturing method and corrosion affect the choice

questions.text: Which CAD or analysis software have you used, and what did you make with it?
covers: The tools and how well you know each
A part, assembly or analysis you made
How you checked the result made sense

questions.text: Tell me about yourself and why you want a core engineering role.
covers: Your degree and the subjects you're strongest in
A project, internship or plant visit that shaped your interest
The kind of mechanical work you want to do

questions.text: Which area of mechanical engineering do you want to work in: design, production, maintenance or something else? Why?
covers: One area, chosen honestly
An experience that drew you to it
What you'd want to learn in your first year

questions.text: Are you comfortable working on a plant floor or site, in shifts, or in another city?
covers: An honest answer, with any limits stated clearly
Any shop-floor or site experience you already have
Why hands-on work matters early in a mechanical career

tips: Revise the subjects most interviews touch: strength of materials, thermodynamics, manufacturing, machine design, fluid mechanics and engineering drawing.
Link each concept to a machine or part you've seen; interviewers commonly ask where it applies.
Know your project in depth: the calculations, the material and why you chose it, and what failed.
If you visited a plant or did an internship, be ready to describe the processes and the safety rules you saw.
For design roles, brush up on drawings and a CAD tool; for maintenance roles, on bearings, pumps, lubrication and root-cause analysis.
Say your assumptions out loud when you estimate or calculate.
